A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same wireframe-metric study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete supplementary materials are readable and support comparison across relocated and renumbered content.

before.justification: v1 reports original human preference annotations, metric and VLM comparisons, learned-metric cross-validation results, and empirical metric-property tests.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results, revises reported rankings and agreement scores, and adds annotation-sample adequacy analyses.

M1.justification: The proposed learned metric still uses rendered wireframes, DINOv2 features, an MLP scoring head, and Bradley–Terry cross-entropy supervision. Added notation and explanations do not establish changes to its architecture, objective, or procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use S23DR reconstructions, PC2WF variants, the same four synthetic corruption families, the same annotator groups, and 128 ground-truth wireframes for property tests. Newly specifying ten houses clarifies existing coverage rather than establishing a new dataset or scenario.

E2.justification: The supplementary group comparison adds an evaluated entry named edge_corner_f1 in v2 Figure 10, absent from v1 Figure 9. The other metric and VLM comparator lists and Table 1 reconstruction entries are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds an evaluation protocol that varies the numbers of raters, comparisons, and houses and compares subset rankings with full-data rankings using Kendall correlation. The existing learned-metric cross-validation and property-test protocols remain unchanged; the exhaustive annotation counts are newly disclosed details.

E4.justification: Section 4 adds substantial validation of whether the central rankings are stable with fewer raters, comparisons, or houses, alongside majority-error and win-rate convergence plots in Figure 5. The factor-analysis explained-variance assessment is removed. The existing metric-property tests remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Beyond v1's agreement and self-consistency summaries, v2 specifies 500 resamples per sample size and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for Kendall correlation. It also reports modeled panel-error probabilities, introducing substantial uncertainty assessment without establishing additional training runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 and agreement/ranking figures contain substantive revisions: perturb med's empirical win rate changes from 0.82 to 0.85, and corner F1 replaces the learned metric atop the CV-group ranking. The reported SVD–BT correlation bound changes from >0.93 to >0.7, while the 85%/5% explained-variance findings disappear. New adequacy results identify thresholds of 3350 comparisons, four houses, and eight raters. These are revised or added findings, not established same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: v2 adds probabilistic majority-vote reasoning assuming a latent correct winner and independent raters with common accuracy. Existing metric definitions and Bradley–Terry equations remain equivalent; the new supplementary spectral-distance section repeats mathematics already present in v1.

C1.justification: The five stated contributions retain their meaning, including human preference evaluation, metric-property tests, a learned metric, and practical recommendations. Both conclusions recommend combining edge- and corner-based metrics and caution against relying solely on learned judging. The cluster finding remains in Section 4 despite its removal from the conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 adds an argument that the annotation sample is sufficient for stable rankings and qualifies the OpenAI/Grok exceptions as only slightly better than chance. Existing explanations concerning recall, editable reconstructions, WED's limitations, and reward hacking are retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds a source-code URL and specifies 3510 comparisons per rater across 27 reconstruction entries and ten houses, plus a 5% self-consistency-check probability. Supplementary Section 6 newly documents recruitment, compensation, break prompts, and annotation duration. These clarify the existing study rather than establish changed settings.

R1.justification: Both versions cite the same 36 works and retain the same positioning relative to reconstruction benchmarks, existing metrics, pretrained visual features, and preference models. Reference differences concern citation locations rather than added research.

P1.justification: v2 makes sentence-level edits, introduces subheadings for the three ranking approaches, reorders observation boxes, and expands the supplementary structure. Smoothness is renamed quasi-proportionality without changing its tests. The overall narrative and main section sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds the three-panel Figure 5, reformats two four-panel figures from 2-by-2 grids into horizontal rows, and relocates the supplementary ranking plot onto a separate page with an additional metric entry. Existing tables, heatmaps, and wireframe illustrations largely retain their display formats.

improvement.justification: The new sample-adequacy analysis, clearer annotation specification, and code-access information make the study easier to assess and reproduce. The gain is limited by unexplained numerical revisions and the new reliability discussion's use of 17 total raters despite the listed groups totaling 18. The core method and recommendations remain stable.
